::: {.chapter-goal}
#### In this chapter
You will separate genuine change from the seasons with harmonic regression, first on synthetic data and then on a real pixel cleared for Indonesia's new capital; turn residuals into alerts with persistence rules; map change from radar, which sees through cloud; count change with Dynamic World without fooling yourself; and measure who was inside the changed ground after the 2018 Palu disaster.
:::


## Harmonic regression, in fifteen lines

A cloud screened optical time series over the tropics arrives as an irregular scatter of observations with a strong annual cycle in it. The problem this creates is that any two dates you happen to compare differ for two reasons at once: the season moved, and possibly the land changed. Separating those is the whole task.

Harmonic regression does it by fitting the season explicitly. Regress NDVI on an intercept, a linear trend, and one or more sine and cosine pairs at the annual frequency. The fitted curve is phenology. What is left over, the residual, is everything phenology does not explain, and that is where change lives.

```{python}
#| label: fig-harmonic-fit
#| fig-cap: "Four years of synthetic NDVI, cloud gaps included, with a two term harmonic fit. The model was fitted only to observations before the dashed line, so what happens after it is prediction rather than description. Drag to zoom; double click to reset."
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import booklib as bk

EVENT = 2.3      # a clearing event, in years from the start of the series
t, ndvi = bk.synthetic_ndvi(n_years=4, disturbance_at=EVENT, seed=7)

# Fit on the period before the event only. A model fitted across a
# disturbance absorbs the disturbance into its own trend term and then
# reports no anomaly, which is the most common way this analysis fails.
before = t < EVENT
coef, predict = bk.harmonic_fit(t[before], ndvi[before], order=2)

smooth = np.linspace(t.min(), t.max(), 400)

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_scatter(x=t, y=ndvi, mode="markers", name="Observations",
                marker=dict(size=7, color=bk.BRIGHT),
                hovertemplate="NDVI %{y:.3f} at year %{x:.2f}<extra></extra>")
fig.add_scatter(x=smooth, y=predict(smooth), mode="lines",
                name="Harmonic fit, pre event",
                line=dict(color=bk.AMBER, width=2.5),
                hovertemplate="expected %{y:.3f}<extra></extra>")
fig.add_vline(x=EVENT, line_dash="dash", line_color=bk.RED,
              annotation_text="clearing", annotation_position="top left")
fig.update_xaxes(title="Years from start of series")
fig.update_yaxes(title="NDVI")
bk.show(fig, height=400)
```

The fit tracks the seasonal rise and fall closely and then, after the dashed line, keeps predicting the vegetation that is no longer there. That divergence is the detection.

Now plot what the model could not explain. This is the step that turns a chart a human reads into a rule a machine can apply.

```{python}
#| label: fig-harmonic-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Residuals from the same fit. Before the event they scatter around zero with a standard deviation of about 0.02 NDVI. After it they sit far below zero and stay there, which is what distinguishes a change from a bad observation."
residual = ndvi - predict(t)
sd = float(residual[before].std())

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_scatter(x=t, y=residual, mode="markers+lines", name="Residual",
                marker=dict(size=6, color=bk.TEAL), line=dict(width=1, color="#c9c4bb"),
                hovertemplate="residual %{y:+.3f} at year %{x:.2f}<extra></extra>")
for k, dash in [(2, "dot"), (3, "dash")]:
    fig.add_hline(y=-k * sd, line_dash=dash, line_color=bk.MUTED,
                  annotation_text=f"-{k} sd", annotation_position="right")
fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="#c9c4bb")
fig.add_vline(x=EVENT, line_dash="dash", line_color=bk.RED)
fig.update_xaxes(title="Years from start of series")
fig.update_yaxes(title="Observed minus expected NDVI")
bk.show(fig, height=360)

print(f"residual sd before the event   {sd:.4f}")
print(f"mean residual after the event  {residual[~before].mean():+.3f}"
      f"  ({abs(residual[~before].mean()) / sd:.0f} standard deviations)")
```

The mean residual after the event is about fifteen standard deviations below zero. That is not a threshold anyone needs to tune; it is a signal that stands clear of the noise by an order of magnitude, which is what a well specified seasonal model buys you.

Three cautions before this becomes an alert, and each one is a section in the prose to come.

A single anomalous observation is not change. Cloud shadow, a missed cirrus, a sensor artefact: all produce one bad point. Requiring persistence, typically three consecutive observations beyond the threshold, removes almost all of them and costs a few weeks of latency.

The threshold belongs to the pixel, not to the landscape. A pixel with noisy history needs a wider band than a stable one, which is why the standard deviation above is computed from the pixel's own residuals rather than fixed globally.

And a drop is not a cause. Harvest, fire, flooding, illegal clearing and a dry season all push NDVI down. The time series says when and how much; it does not say what happened, and a report that skips that distinction is not defensible.

::: {.py-live}
```python
# A harmonic fit with nothing but the standard library, so the mechanism is
# visible. Three unknowns: mean level, and one sine and cosine pair.
import math

# Twelve monthly NDVI observations over one year.
months = list(range(12))
ndvi = [0.62, 0.64, 0.71, 0.78, 0.82, 0.84,
        0.83, 0.79, 0.74, 0.69, 0.65, 0.62]

def design(m):
    x = m / 12.0
    return [1.0, math.sin(2 * math.pi * x), math.cos(2 * math.pi * x)]

# Normal equations, solved by Gaussian elimination. Three by three, by hand.
A = [[sum(design(m)[i] * design(m)[j] for m in months) for j in range(3)]
     + [sum(design(m)[i] * ndvi[m] for m in months)] for i in range(3)]

for i in range(3):
    A[i] = [v / A[i][i] for v in A[i]]
    for k in range(3):
        if k != i:
            A[k] = [a - A[k][i] * b for a, b in zip(A[k], A[i])]

c = [A[i][3] for i in range(3)]
amplitude = math.hypot(c[1], c[2])

print(f"mean NDVI        {c[0]:.3f}")
print(f"seasonal amplitude {amplitude:.3f}   (peak to trough {2 * amplitude:.3f})\n")

for m in months:
    fit = sum(ci * di for ci, di in zip(c, design(m)))
    r = ndvi[m] - fit
    flag = "  <-- check this one" if abs(r) > 0.03 else ""
    print(f"month {m + 1:2d}  observed {ndvi[m]:.2f}  expected {fit:.3f}  residual {r:+.3f}{flag}")

# Try this: drop month 9 to 0.45, as a clearing would, and run again. The
# residual for that month goes far outside the others, and the fit itself
# barely moves, because one point among twelve cannot pull it. That
# asymmetry is what makes residuals a usable detector.
```
:::


## From synthetic to real: a pixel cleared for the new capital

The synthetic series shows the mechanism under ideal conditions. Real data adds two complications: gaps where clouds hid the ground, and a training period that is shorter than you would like. The next listing takes one 10 m pixel in the core zone of Nusantara, Indonesia's new capital in East Kalimantan, that was vegetated in 2019 and is bare or built today, and runs the same three steps on every clear Sentinel-2 observation from 2019 to 2024.

{{< include _snippets/ch21_harmonic_alerts.qmd >}}

**Fit the season on years you trust.** Cloud-screened Sentinel-2 surface reflectance only begins here in 2019, so the season is learned from 2019-2020, 58 clear observations. The first version of this script also fitted a linear trend. With so short a training period the trend term extrapolated the season upwards, predicting an NDVI of 1.2 by 2024, which is impossible, and every later observation then looked like a loss: it raised an "alert" in 2021, two years before anything happened. Without the trend term the model is a season and nothing else, and the residuals in the fit period scatter with a standard deviation of 0.034 NDVI.

**Turn residuals into an alert with a persistence rule.** One observation far below the season can be haze or a cloud shadow the mask missed. The rule here waits for three consecutive observations below -3 standard deviations. At this pixel the first such observation is on 6 March 2023, and the alert fires on 8 March 2023, when clearing for the capital reached it. The same rule raises no alert inside the fit period. Persistence costs time: where clear observations are weeks apart, waiting for three can delay an alert by months, which is the trade-off every operational system (GLAD, RADD, DIST-ALERT) tunes.

## Every pixel at once, and a second opinion from radar

The same harmonic model can be fitted to every pixel with one Earth Engine reducer (`ee.Reducer.linearRegression`), and the mean 2023 residual of each pixel, in units of its own residual standard deviation, becomes a change map. On the map, the optical change traces exactly what is known to have happened: a grid of new roads in the south-west and the cleared blocks of the government core around 116.70° E, 0.97° S, 1,257 ha in the 100 km² box. A minimum mapping unit of 0.1 ha removes isolated pixels and changes the total little (1,220 ha), because construction clears large connected areas.

Radar answers the same question differently. The **log ratio** of Sentinel-1 VH backscatter, 2023 against 2019 (the difference in decibels), flags a change of more than 3 dB on 563 ha. Radar sees through cloud, so it needs no screening and no season model, but it responds to anything that changes the surface's structure or moisture. Most of its change is not where the optical change is: the two agree on only 102 ha, and much of the radar-only change lies along the river and wetland in the north, where water levels, not clearing, move the backscatter. Checked against Dynamic World, which changed label on 10 % of the box, the optical change is enriched (27 % of it coincides with a label change), the radar change less so (19 %). Here the optical harmonic map is the better product; in a cloudier season the radar would be the only one available.

**Test the rule on a year when nothing should happen.** The fairest check of a change rule is to run it on a period with no change. Fitted on 2019 alone, the same rule flags 1,663 ha in 2023, but also 1,028 ha in 2020, before clearing reached most of the box. With one year of training, more than half of the "change" could be noise: one year is not enough to learn a season, and a plantation harvest or a dry year looks like a disturbance to a model that has seen only one cycle. Every change map should carry a test like this before its area is quoted.

## From change to alert, and the methods that do it at scale

Operational alert systems formalise the steps of this chapter:

- **Breakpoint methods** fit the season and look for the date when a new segment starts. **CCDC** (Continuous Change Detection and Classification, `ee.Algorithms.TemporalSegmentation.Ccdc`) fits harmonic segments to every pixel and reports break dates; **LandTrendr** fits piecewise-linear segments to annual composites; **BFAST** tests for breaks in trend and season separately.
- **Alert rules** add a minimum mapping unit, a persistence or confirmation rule (two of three, or three in a row) and an expiry for unconfirmed alerts.
- **Validation** samples alerts and non-alerts and checks them in very high resolution imagery, giving commission and omission rates (Chapter [-@sec-accuracy]).

The details differ; the logic is the one built here: model what is normal, measure departure from it, and require the departure to persist.

## Counting change with Dynamic World

Dynamic World labels every Sentinel-2 scene with nine class probabilities, which makes it the fastest way to count change. It is also an easy way to fool yourself. This listing comes from the GEE101 Lampung exercise, with one correction: the original extracted built-up land with class 2, which in Dynamic World is grass. Look at the chart before the maps. A yearly number that halves and then doubles is telling you about the data, not the town.

{{< include _snippets/ch21_dynamic_world_change.qmd >}}

The chart is the lesson. Built-up area in this Lampung box goes from 5.5 km² in 2019 to 2.0 km² in 2020 and back to 5.4 km² in 2021, which no town does. The column of scene counts explains part of it: the yearly label is the most frequent label among however many clear scenes that year happened to have, and a year with few or seasonally clustered scenes gives a different answer from the same ground. The stricter probability rule (built-up probability above a threshold) is lower every year but jumps in the same years, so it is not a cure. Two habits make Dynamic World usable for change: compare the same season in both years, and smooth over several years before differencing, so that one odd year does not create change that never happened.

## A disaster seen twice: Palu, 2018

Change detection at its most direct is two images and a question: what is different, and who was there? On 28 September 2018 an earthquake liquefied whole neighbourhoods of Palu and a tsunami struck the bay shore. This listing, from the GEE101 Palu exercise rebuilt on public data, maps both. It separates them by distance from the sea and counts the buildings and people inside each zone.

{{< include _snippets/ch21_palu_liquefaction.qmd >}}

Two very different processes leave the same signature in a before-and-after pair: vegetation and roofs gone, bright bare ground in their place. Distance from the shore separates them. Inland, the liquefaction flow slides, Petobo the largest in this scene, turned 239 ha into bare mud, with 322 mapped buildings and about 2,400 people (WorldPop 2018) inside. Within 500 m of the bay the tsunami left 17 ha of new bare ground, with 32 buildings and about 170 people. The tsunami zone is underestimated by this method: water damage that leaves a roof standing does not change the image much. A difference map counts what it can see; a damage assessment has to say what it cannot.

## Verdict: how far to trust this, and how to make it accurate

**Verdict.** Harmonic models and radar log ratios are fast and transparent, and the single-pixel alert fired when the clearing happened. The regional map is **not yet trustworthy as an area**: the stable-year test shows that a one-year season model flags much ground that did not change.

**How to make it accurate:**

1. **Fit the season on several stable years** (three or more), so that the model has seen dry and wet years.
2. **Validate alerts** against very high resolution imagery or field checks on a sample of alerts and non-alerts, and report commission and omission errors.
3. **Combine optical and radar** with a confirmation rule, so that cloud does not delay alerts and moisture does not create them.
4. **Use an established alert system** (GLAD, RADD, DIST-ALERT) as a baseline and show what your local method adds.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Change the persistence rule from three consecutive observations to two of three. How much earlier does the alert at the capital pixel fire, and does the fit period now raise a false alert?
2. Fit the regional model on 2019-2021 instead of 2019-2020. Does the 2023 change area shrink, and why might it?
3. Repeat the radar change with ascending and descending orbits combined. Does the agreement with the optical map improve?
4. Smooth the Dynamic World built-up series over three years before differencing. Does the 2020 dip disappear?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

**1.** With two of three observations below −3 SD, the alert can fire on the second low observation instead of the third, so it comes one revisit earlier at most, a few days at this pixel's observation spacing (the chapter's alert came two days after the first low observation, 6 to 8 March 2023). The cost is more false alerts: two low values in three is easier for haze or a missed cloud shadow to produce. Check the fit period: if any alert appears in 2019-2020, the looser rule is too permissive for this series.

**2.** Usually yes. Adding 2021 lengthens the training period, so the harmonic fit is more stable and the residual standard deviation larger and more realistic; a 2023 observation must then fall further from the season to count, and the change area shrinks. It can also shrink because some clearing began in 2021, so that disturbance becomes part of the "normal" the model learns: the price of a longer fit is a baseline that may already contain change.

**3.** Usually not. Mixing ascending and descending passes adds a viewing-geometry difference to the log ratio: slopes facing one pass look brighter, the other darker, and the mix of passes differs between years. That produces change where nothing changed, especially on the hilly terrain around the capital, so agreement with the optical map tends to fall. Keep one orbit direction.

**4.** Smoothing with a three-year moving mean (or median) before differencing damps a one-year anomaly, so the 2020 dip shrinks a lot or disappears: it was most likely a classification artefact of that year rather than real loss of buildings. The cost is that genuine change is spread over three years and its timing blurs. A median is better than a mean at removing a single bad year.
:::
